title: Bilevel Graph Structure Learning, Revisited: Inner-Channel Origins of the Reported Gain

paper.title: Bilevel Graph Structure Learning, Revisited: Inner-Channel Origins of the Reported Gain
paper.abstract: Abstract Bilevel graph structure learning is widely understood to improve graph neural networks by jointly optimizing model parameters and a learned graph structure, with the resulting performance gain attributed to the rewired adjacency. We find that this attribution may be overstated: training-dynamics effects in the inner loop, rather than the rewiring itself, capture a substantial share of the gain. To establish this, we introduce frozen- ϕ \phi , a control that freezes the graph while retaining the inner-loop training schedule. This decomposes the bilevel gain into an inner channel of T T -step training dynamics with implicit gradient regularization and a graph channel of the graph rewiring itself. On spatio-temporal flow forecasting the inner channel matches or exceeds the full bilevel pipeline, accounting for 78 78 – 101 % 101\% of the gain; on node classification it accounts for 37 37 – 44 % 44\% under a Bernoulli edge-level parameterization. We also verify that classical spectral diagnostics can dissociate from task gain. We propose frozen- ϕ \phi as a standardized diagnostic for bilevel graph structure learning, with graph distillation as a method-agnostic complement. A three-precondition framework further predicts the sign of the bilevel gain on all six benchmarks.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Bilevel graph structure learning (GSL) optimizes the graph and the model jointly through an outer loop on a validation objective, and the learned adjacency is credited with the resulting improvement [ 13 , 6 ] . The bilevel procedure differs from vanilla training in two ways that could each account for its reported gain. The first is graph modification, executed by the outer loop. The second is an inner loop that runs T T gradient steps per outer iteration, which has known implicit regularization properties [ 4 , 33 ] unrelated to the graph. Existing evaluations treat the bilevel gain as flowing entirely from the first mechanism. We ask whether this attribution is correct. We introduce the frozen- ϕ \phi control : the same bilevel training loop, with the same T T -step inner optimization and warmup schedule, but with the graph parameter ϕ \phi held fixed at its initial value. The control isolates extended inner optimization from graph modification, holding every other variable constant. This is the GSL analogue of the frozen-controller experiments that prompted reassessment of attribution in neural architecture search, where freezing the architecture parameter while preserving the training pipeline revealed that pipeline choices, rather than searched architectures, explained much of the gain [ 19 , 40 ] . Our goal is to reframe which component of bilevel GSL is actually responsible for the improvement. A productive theoretical framework has characterized over-squashing through graph curvature [ 35 ] , commute time and effective resistance [ 11 , 5 ] , and the spatio-temporal Jacobian factorization for decoupled STGNNs [ 27 ] . Our decomposition is complementary to this framework: the over-squashing bounds describe worst-case sensitivity propagation between nodes, while our control measures how much of bilevel’s empirical performance lift is attributable to graph modification at all.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: Our contributions are as follows. 1. We show that, across both spatio-temporal flow forecasting and node classification, a substantial fraction of reported bilevel-GSL gains is attributable to inner-loop training dynamics rather than to the learned graph structure, with the inner channel accounting for 78 78 – 101 % 101\% on flow forecasting and 37 37 – 44 % 44\% on node classification. 2. We corroborate this attribution through three independent diagnostics (edge corruption that varies graph quality, alternative training schedules including weight decay and end-to-end joint training, and convergent triangulation on PeMS07), complemented by a T T -sweep that distinguishes two inner-loop training regimes (mini-batch reuse versus full-batch reset), all unified by an implicit-gradient-regularization mechanism. 3. We propose frozen- ϕ \phi as a standardized diagnostic for gradient-based bilevel GSL that modifies rather than replaces the initial adjacency, with graph distillation as a method-agnostic complement, accompanied by a three-precondition framework on the predefined adjacency that predicts when bilevel rewiring helps.

sections.heading: What this paper does not claim.
sections.text: We do not claim that learned graph structure is useless in bilevel GSL, nor that bilevel methods cannot be improved; we claim that, under standard reporting practice, the inner loop’s contribution to measured gains is much larger than typically credited.

sections.heading: Bilevel and related graph structure learning.
sections.text: Bilevel GSL parameterizes the adjacency jointly with model weights via nested optimization with an outer validation objective. LDS [ 13 ] introduced a per-edge Bernoulli parameterization; IDGL [ 6 ] iteratively learns a continuous adjacency from multi-head weighted cosine similarity of node embeddings under a single (non-nested) training objective. GEN [ 38 ] uses EM-based alternation, and Pro-GNN [ 17 ] couples graph learning with adversarial defense (gains primarily on perturbed graphs). LCGS [ 15 ] is the closest prior bilevel method using a continuous (dual-normalized) adjacency rather than LDS’s Bernoulli parameterization, with head-to-head comparison against LDS on Cora and Citeseer. Single-level alternatives [ 12 , 25 , 32 ] and ST-domain analogues [ 16 , 42 , 34 , 10 , 26 ] use joint training rather than bilevel optimization. Adaptive STGNNs internalize graph learning into the forward pass: AGCRN [ 2 ] uses an embedding-based internal adjacency, while GraphWaveNet [ 39 ] uses such an internal matrix alongside diffusion (random-walk normalized) transitions of a pre-defined adjacency. The frozen- ϕ \phi decomposition is defined specifically for bilevel GSL with gradient-based outer updates and incremental graph modification (Section 3 ); single-level and adaptive approaches lie outside this scope.

sections.heading: Over-squashing and graph rewiring.
sections.text: Alon and Yahav [1] identified over-squashing in message-passing networks. Subsequent theory connected the phenomenon to graph curvature [ 35 ] , information contraction [ 3 ] , commute time [ 11 ] , and effective resistance [ 5 ] , motivating task-agnostic rewiring preprocessors [ 14 , 18 , 28 , 5 ] . Tori et al. [36] found that curvature-based rewiring gains often reflect hyperparameter sweep outliers, underscoring the importance of controlled evaluation. Marisca et al. [27] extended the framework to spatio-temporal GNNs with a layer-wise multiplicative Jacobian factorization for time-then-space and time-and-space architectures, the structural foundation on which our architectural scope conditions rest. Our methodology shares the controlled-evaluation principle of Tori et al. [36] but isolates a distinct confound: the inner-loop training schedule, rather than hyperparameter sensitivity, in the bilevel optimization regime.

sections.heading: The attribution gap.
sections.text: No prior study has isolated the contribution of graph modification from the training dynamics introduced by bilevel optimization, despite extensive theoretical and empirical work on graph rewiring. Recent benchmarks [ 21 , 44 ] independently observe that GSL methods do not consistently outperform vanilla GNN counterparts on standard benchmarks, but do not identify the mechanism. The frozen- ϕ \phi control fills this gap: it provides the first decomposition that separates training dynamics from graph modification within bilevel GSL.

sections.heading: 3.2 Definition and three-way comparison
sections.text: Following the principle of freezing the outer parameter while preserving the inner training pipeline, used as a diagnostic ablation in neural architecture search [ 19 , 40 ] , we define the frozen- ϕ \phi control for bilevel GSL. The frozen- ϕ \phi control is the ablation in which the outer update is disabled while the T T -step inner loop is retained in full: ϕ \phi is held at its initialization throughout training and θ \theta is optimized by exactly the same inner procedure used in the full bilevel method. We refer to the contribution of inner-loop training under a fixed graph as the inner channel , and the contribution of graph modification by the outer loop as the graph channel . sections.heading: 3.4 Scope conditions
sections.text: The frozen- ϕ \phi decomposition applies under three conditions: (i) the bilevel procedure uses a gradient-based outer update with ϕ \phi parameterizing the graph continuously or via reparameterized discrete variables; (ii) the graph is modified incrementally from A init A_{\mathrm{init}} rather than replaced from scratch; and (iii) the backbone consumes an external adjacency. LDS [ 13 ] and our spatio-temporal bilevel implementation satisfy all three. IDGL [ 6 ] (single-level) violates (i); GEN [ 38 ] (EM-based replacement) violates (ii); Pro-GNN [ 17 ] produces negative clean-graph gain on Cora, leaving the share decomposition undefined (Appendix V ). Coupled backbones such as DCRNN [ 20 ] embed spatial aggregation inside GRU gates, falling outside the regime where the factored Jacobian of Marisca et al. [27] is structurally guaranteed; adaptive backbones pose a structural exclusion of (iii), since AGCRN [ 2 ] uses only an internal adaptive matrix and GraphWaveNet [ 39 ] learns an internal one alongside the external adjacency. We therefore restrict the frozen- ϕ \phi analysis to decoupled polynomial-filter backbones (DiffConv, ChebConv, MPGRU). For node classification, we evaluate on Cora and Citeseer, on which LDS has a published and validated configuration; heterophilous benchmarks [ 30 ] fall outside our scope: no validated bilevel GSL configuration exists, and tuning from scratch would risk the hyperparameter confound of Tori et al. [36] .

sections.heading: Method-agnostic complement.
sections.text: For methods outside the frozen- ϕ \phi scope, graph distillation provides a complementary diagnostic: transfer A ϕ A_{\phi} from a completed GSL run into vanilla training of a target backbone and measure improvement over A init A_{\mathrm{init}} . The two diagnostics measure different quantities: distillation conflates graph modification with graph-model co-adaptation by re-training θ \theta from scratch on A ϕ A_{\phi} , while frozen- ϕ \phi holds the inner-loop schedule fixed and isolates only the graph modification. Distillation has weaker resolution than frozen- ϕ \phi but applies to any GSL method producing positive gain on a clean graph, and is therefore the appropriate diagnostic when frozen- ϕ \phi is inapplicable (Appendix P ).

sections.text: We formulate task-aligned rewiring as bilevel optimization: min ϕ ⁡ ℒ val ​ ( θ ∗ ​ ( ϕ ) , A ϕ ) s . t . θ ∗ ​ ( ϕ ) = arg ⁡ min θ ​ ℒ train ​ ( θ , A ϕ ) , \min_{\phi}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}(\theta^{*}(\phi),A_{\phi})\quad\mathrm{s.t.}\quad\theta^{*}(\phi)=\arg\min_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\theta,A_{\phi}), (4) where a policy π ϕ \pi_{\phi} reweights the adjacency: A ϕ = A ⊙ softmax row ​ ( W ϕ ) A_{\phi}=A\odot\mathrm{softmax}_{\mathrm{row}}(W_{\phi}) , preserving sparsity and degree normalization in the spatio-temporal regime. We use Liu et al. [24] ’s first-order approximation ( ξ = 0 \xi=0 ): the inner-loop θ \theta updates treat A ϕ A_{\phi} as detached from the computation graph, and the outer gradient is evaluated as ∇ ϕ ℒ val ​ ( θ , A ϕ ) \nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}(\theta,A_{\phi}) at the resulting θ \theta without backpropagating through the inner trajectory. For node classification we use LDS [ 13 ] with its Bernoulli edge parameterization, full-batch inner updates, and GCN inner parameters reset per outer iteration. The full algorithm is in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Datasets and backbones.
sections.text: Spatio-temporal experiments use the Torch Spatiotemporal framework [ 7 ] on six benchmarks (PeMS04/07/08 flow, METR-LA and PeMS-BAY speed, AirQuality). Primary backbone is DiffConv ( K = 2 K{=}2 bidirectional diffusion, the standard configuration); ChebConv and MPGRU are decoupled secondary backbones, DCRNN [ 20 ] is the coupled backbone, and AGCRN and GraphWaveNet are adaptive references (Section 3.4 ). Node classification uses the GSLB fork [ 21 ] with LDS on Cora and Citeseer (homophilous, the regime where LDS was validated); the GCN inner backbone uses GSLB’s per-dataset tuned configuration (hidden 128 128 on Cora, 64 64 on Citeseer).

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: ST runs report 5 seeds, NC runs 10 seeds, with T = 10 T=10 inner steps for ST (100 epochs) and T = 5 T=5 for NC (GSLB default). We report mean ± \pm std with paired t t -tests for channel decompositions. Full setup, seed lists, and statistical reporting conventions are in Appendices C , D , Z .

sections.heading: 5.1 Does spatial rewiring improve spatio-temporal forecasting?
sections.text: Across six datasets with the DiffConv backbone (full results in Appendix Table 8 ), bilevel achieves 3.8 3.8 – 6.4 % 6.4\% MAE improvement on flow datasets (PeMS04/07/08) with non-overlapping seed distributions, while static rewiring methods (FoSR, BORF, SDRF, GTR) are within noise of vanilla on all six datasets, consistent with prior work on static rewiring [ 36 ] . On speed datasets, the pattern diverges: PeMS-BAY shows a modest − 0.7 % -0.7\% while METR-LA shows + 2.5 % +2.5\% (bilevel actively harms performance). We return to this split in Section 5.4 .

sections.heading: The inner channel accounts for 78 78 – 101 % 101\% on flow datasets.
sections.text: Freezing ϕ \phi while retaining T = 10 T=10 accounts for 78%, 101%, and 81% of the full bilevel improvement on PeMS04, PeMS07, and PeMS08 respectively. PeMS07 is extreme: frozen- ϕ \phi and bilevel test MAEs differ by 0.009 0.009 , well within the per-seed standard deviation ( σ ≈ 0.035 \sigma\approx 0.035 , Table 1 ); the graph-channel point estimate is statistically indistinguishable from zero. The seed distributions for frozen- ϕ \phi and vanilla are clearly separated on PeMS07 and PeMS08 and nearly separated on PeMS04 (Appendix H ). On METR-LA and AirQuality bilevel does not improve over vanilla ( Δ total ≤ 0 \Delta_{\mathrm{total}}\leq 0 ). On PeMS-BAY the bilevel improvement over vanilla is small ( − 0.011 -0.011 MAE) and the inner and graph channels carry opposite signs (frozen- ϕ \phi is slightly worse than vanilla, while bilevel recovers); we therefore mark its decomposition as n/a in Table 1 and examine all three scope-boundary cases in Section 5.4 . We additionally evaluate the frozen- ϕ \phi decomposition on node classification with LDS [ 13 ] on Cora and Citeseer. The choice of LDS is structural: frozen- ϕ \phi requires gradient-based bilevel optimization, incremental modification of an initial adjacency, and positive empirical gain on the clean graph (Section 3.4 ). Among published GSL methods for node classification, only LDS satisfies all three; GEN [ 38 ] uses EM-based replacement of the adjacency rather than incremental modification, Pro-GNN [ 17 ] is designed for adversarial defense and produces negative clean-graph gain ( Δ total = − 3.66 \Delta_{\text{total}}=-3.66 pp on Cora), and IDGL [ 6 ] is single-level. The graph-distillation complement (Appendix P ) extends the analysis to methods outside this scope. We treat NC as a parameterization-robustness check across a distinct training regime (full-batch reset vs. mini-batch reuse) and ST as the primary regime.

sections.heading: 5.3 Two training regimes produce distinct mechanistic signatures
sections.text: Varying T T provides mechanistic evidence for Proposition 1 : the mini-batch reuse regime predicts the frozen- ϕ \phi loss depends on T T ; the full-batch reset regime predicts it is invariant past inner convergence. We sweep T ∈ { 1 , 3 , 5 , 10 , 20 } T\in\{1,3,5,10,20\} in both regimes (Figure 2 ; numerical values in Appendix D ).

sections.heading: Mini-batch reuse drives T T -dependence; full-batch reset yields T T -invariance.
sections.text: On PeMS04, three predictions of Proposition 1 hold: at T = 1 T=1 the frozen- ϕ \phi MAE matches vanilla within 0.001 0.001 , well below the per-seed noise floor of σ ≈ 0.04 \sigma\approx 0.04 (Table 4 ); frozen- ϕ \phi MAE decreases monotonically with T T through T = 10 T=10 as R IGR ∝ T R_{\mathrm{IGR}}\propto T grows; full bilevel tracks frozen- ϕ \phi at every T T offset by a small approximately T T -independent graph-channel contribution. On Cora and Citeseer the frozen- ϕ \phi accuracy is instead nearly flat across T ∈ { 3 , 5 , 10 , 20 } T\in\{3,5,10,20\} while full bilevel maintains higher accuracy than frozen- ϕ \phi at every T T (clearly improving with T T on Citeseer; within seed noise on Cora), the predicted full-batch reset signature (per-outer-iteration parameter reset collapses the inner trajectory to a T T -invariant function past convergence). Figure 2 : Two training regimes produce distinct mechanistic signatures. (a) On PeMS04, frozen- ϕ \phi MAE decreases monotonically with T T as R IGR ∝ T R_{\mathrm{IGR}}\propto T accumulates within reused mini-batches; at T = 1 T=1 frozen- ϕ \phi collapses to vanilla. (b) On Cora and Citeseer, frozen- ϕ \phi accuracy is T T -invariant past inner convergence: full-batch gradients with per-outer-iteration parameter reset render the inner trajectory T T -independent. Both signatures match the predictions of Proposition 1 .

sections.heading: 5.4 Triangulation and scope across regimes
sections.text: Three independent diagnostics, edge corruption on Cora, alternative training schedules on PeMS04, and convergent triangulation on PeMS07, corroborate the inner-channel attribution and delineate where the graph channel becomes operative. The unified six-dataset interpretation through three preconditions on the predefined adjacency is developed in Section 6 and Appendix X .

sections.heading: Graph quality determines channel balance.

The channel share crosses 50/50 near r = 0.50 r=0.50 and ends graph-dominated at r = 0.75 r=0.75 ; all channel tests reach p < 0.001 p<0.001 at every r ≥ 0.10 r\geq 0.10 . Graph quality, operationalized through controlled corruption, directly determines the channel balance within a single regime: the inner channel saturates at an architecture-dependent ceiling while the graph channel scales with structural slack. The same logic applies to ST: distance-based adjacencies are not optimized for the forecasting task and exhibit large task-initial mismatch, similar to the corrupted Cora regime.

sections.heading: Weight decay and end-to-end joint training do not replicate the inner channel.
sections.text: Explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization on PeMS04 with λ ∈ { 10 − 4 , 10 − 3 , 10 − 2 } \lambda\in\{10^{-4},10^{-3},10^{-2}\} does not close the gap (Appendix F , Table 6 ): even the best setting ( λ = 10 − 4 \lambda=10^{-4} ) is marginally worse than vanilla, while frozen- ϕ \phi at T = 10 T=10 achieves an approximately 0.91 0.91 MAE improvement over vanilla. The IGR mechanism of Proposition 1 involves gradient norms and stochastic variance rather than parameter norms. A 10 × 10\times -compute vanilla baseline ( 1000 1000 epochs) closes part of the inner-channel gap but leaves the bilevel residual unaffected (Appendix G ), supporting the trajectory-length interpretation of IGR. An end-to-end baseline that jointly optimizes W ϕ W_{\phi} and θ \theta on the training loss without a separate outer loop also fails: on PeMS07 bilevel achieves − 1.43 -1.43 MAE while E2E achieves − 0.07 -0.07 , a twenty-fold gap that cannot be attributed to graph modification (which contributes a near-zero share on PeMS07), leaving the T T -step inner schedule itself as the operative mechanism.

sections.heading: PeMS07: three diagnostics converge on pure training dynamics.
sections.text: We observe a suggestive anti-correlation between modification magnitude and improvement across the six datasets ( ρ = − 0.77 \rho=-0.77 , p = 0.072 p=0.072 , N = 6 N=6 , marginal at conventional thresholds): PeMS07 shows the largest gain ( Δ \Delta MAE = − 6.4 % =-6.4\% ) yet the smallest modifications (99% of edges have | Δ ​ w | < 0.1 |\Delta w|<0.1 ). Three independent diagnostics on PeMS07 all yield small graph-channel point estimates: frozen- ϕ \phi accounts for 101% of the bilevel gain, graph distillation recovers only 1%, and end-to-end reweighting is 20 × 20\times weaker than bilevel (Figure 14 in Appendix Q ). Bilevel’s success regime on flow forecasting is selective minimal intervention, not aggressive structural rewiring (Appendix X.4 ).

sections.heading: The inner channel itself fails on speed signals.
sections.text: Bilevel is neutral on DCRNN and harmful on METR-LA (Appendix N ); frozen- ϕ \phi on METR-LA is also worse than vanilla ( Δ = + 0.052 \Delta=+0.052 MAE, ≈ 5 ​ σ F \approx 5\sigma_{F} ) and on PeMS-BAY marginally worse ( Δ = + 0.005 \Delta=+0.005 , within 1 ​ σ F 1\sigma_{F} ), so the inner channel itself fails on speed signals rather than being canceled by a harmful outer update. Per-distance Jacobian measurements (Appendix L ) show bilevel relaxes the short-to-long sensitivity ratio on five of six datasets, with METR-LA the exception (vanilla 95 × 95\times vs. bilevel 335 × 335\times ), consistent with bilevel actively concentrating propagation in a regime where it harms forecasting.

sections.heading: When does bilevel rewiring help?
sections.text: The six-dataset gain pattern admits a unified explanation through three preconditions on the predefined adjacency: (i) structural slack ( A init A_{\text{init}} is suboptimal for the task-relevant structure), (ii) loss identifiability (the validation loss has informative gradients in ϕ \phi near A init A_{\text{init}} ), and (iii) parametrization expressiveness (the policy class can represent the true dependency); formalized in Appendix X.1 , per-dataset mapping in Table 26 . Flow datasets satisfy all three; speed datasets fail (i)–(ii) because kinematic-wave physics [ 22 ] aligns the distance graph with the dynamics and per-node embeddings absorb the residual variance; AirQuality fails (iii) because the standard distance-based adjacency is block-diagonal with zero inter-city edges (Appendix X.2 ). The framework correctly predicts the sign of the bilevel gain on all six benchmarks, including the three on which bilevel does not improve over the clean-graph baseline; Appendix X.6 summarizes the resulting practitioner decision flow.

sections.heading: Methodological recommendation.
sections.text: We propose the frozen- ϕ \phi ablation as a standard control in graph structure learning. Concretely, any paper reporting gains from a learned graph should report: (i) the frozen- ϕ \phi test metric under the same T T -step inner schedule as the full bilevel method, (ii) the inner share Δ inner / Δ total \Delta_{\mathrm{inner}}/\Delta_{\mathrm{total}} from ( 2 ), (iii) a T T -sweep checking whether the frozen- ϕ \phi result is T T -dependent or T T -invariant. Absent these controls, reported GSL gains are confounded with training dynamics introduced by the inner optimization schedule. For methods outside the scope of the frozen- ϕ \phi control, graph distillation provides a method-agnostic complement (Appendix P ).

sections.heading: Relation to bilevel optimization beyond GSL.
sections.text: Implicit regularization in bilevel optimization has been studied in meta-learning [ 37 , 31 ] . Our contribution is not to discover this phenomenon but to (i) show that it explains a substantial share of gains attributed to graph modification in bilevel GSL, where this attribution has not been previously questioned, and (ii) provide a diagnostic that GSL practitioners can run on their own methods. The diagnostic principle, isolating outer-parameter contribution by freezing the outer parameter while preserving inner-loop training, potentially applies to bilevel optimization beyond GSL, though we leave such extensions to future work.

sections.heading: Spectral metrics dissociate from task gain.
sections.text: A natural alternative explanation for the divergence between bilevel and static rewiring is spectral: that bilevel optimizes a graph-spectral objective (larger spectral gap λ 2 \lambda_{2} or narrower effective spectral support) that static methods do not match. We tested this directly on the LCC-restricted subgraph that every method shares (Appendix M ). The data shows a clean dissociation. GTR is a strong spectral-gap maximizer: λ 2 \lambda_{2} increases by 2.6 2.6 – 15.5 × 15.5\times on every benchmark with a numerically resolved baseline (Table 2 ), yet GTR matches vanilla on test MAE. Bilevel decreases λ 2 \lambda_{2} on four of six datasets and produces the largest forecasting gains on flow (between − 3.8 % -3.8\% and − 6.4 % -6.4\% ) without raising λ 2 \lambda_{2} . Spectral gap optimization is therefore decoupled from task improvement on these benchmarks. sections.heading: Open questions.
sections.text: Several questions remain open. We highlight two: first, whether the three-precondition framework predicts the sign of the graph-channel contribution on heterophilous benchmarks (e.g., Squirrel, Chameleon, Actor); no validated bilevel GSL configuration currently exists in this regime, and applying LDS to heterophilous benchmarks without tuning would risk reproducing the failure mode of Tori et al. [36] . Second, whether discrete-edge bilevel methods designed for ST forecasting [ 32 ] fall under the mini-batch reuse regime (predicting T T -dependent inner-channel gains as in our ST setting) or the full-batch reset regime (predicting T T -invariant frozen- ϕ \phi as in NC); the answer determines whether their reported gains derive from the same training-dynamics mechanism we identify here.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Our findings do not claim the over-squashing bounds of Topping et al. [35] , Di Giovanni et al. [11] , Marisca et al. [27] are incorrect; they bound a different quantity than the practical constraint we identify in spatio-temporal forecasting. Consistent with the diagnostic framing, we identify the confound and provide tools for measuring it; the path to mitigation is left to future work. Our decomposition measures contribution, not necessity, of each channel. NC evaluation is limited to Cora and Citeseer. Bilevel incurs ∼ 15 × \sim 15\times training overhead on PeMS04 DiffConv (Appendix Y ); inference cost is unchanged.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: The frozen- ϕ \phi control isolates the contribution of graph modification within bilevel GSL by freezing the graph while retaining the inner-loop training schedule. On six benchmarks, the inner channel matches or exceeds the full bilevel pipeline on spatio-temporal flow forecasting and accounts for a substantial share of the gain on node classification, indicating that inner-loop training dynamics contribute substantially more to bilevel GSL gains than is typically credited. We propose frozen- ϕ \phi as a standard ablation, with graph distillation as a method-agnostic complement; the diagnostic principle of freezing the outer parameter while preserving inner-loop training may apply to bilevel optimization beyond GSL.

sections.heading: E.2 Gradient Norm Analysis
sections.text: To characterize the inner-step mechanism we instrument the inner loop and record the pre-clipping gradient norm at each step t ∈ { 0 , … , 9 } t\in\{0,\ldots,9\} across the first three epochs on PeMS04 (DiffConv, seed = = 42). Figure 4 shows the within-batch profile averaged over batches in epoch 0, together with per-batch training loss trajectories for five representative batches. Figure 5 shows the same gradient-norm profile stratified by epoch. Figure 4 : PeMS04 (DiffConv, seed = = 42), epoch 0. Left: pre-clipping gradient norm during the inner loop, averaged across batches. The norm is approximately constant across all 10 inner steps, indicating that each step provides a parameter update of comparable magnitude rather than driving per-batch convergence. Right: per-batch training loss over inner steps for five representative batches; loss trajectories are approximately flat or slowly decreasing, confirming that T = 10 T=10 does not produce intra-batch convergence. Figure 5 : Pre-clipping gradient norm across inner steps stratified by epoch (PeMS04, DiffConv, seed = = 42). The overall norm decreases substantially across epochs (epoch 0: ≈ 68 \approx 68 ; epoch 1: ≈ 37 \approx 37 ; epoch 2: ≈ 22 \approx 22 ), but the within-epoch profile remains flat at every epoch. Gradient-norm reduction is driven by inter-epoch learning, not by intra-batch convergence. Two observations follow. First, gradient norms are approximately constant across inner steps within each epoch (Figure 4 , left), ruling out the hypothesis that T = 10 T=10 drives per-batch convergence: if the model were converging on each batch, the within-batch gradient norms would decrease monotonically from step 0 to step 9, but they do not. Each inner step instead provides a parameter update of comparable magnitude. Second, gradient norms decrease substantially across epochs (Figure 5 ), reflecting the normal training-time convergence that occurs in vanilla training as well. The mechanism underlying the inner-channel benefit is therefore accumulated parameter displacement: each batch receives T T gradient steps of similar magnitude in approximately the same direction, yielding a T T -fold larger effective per-batch step relative to vanilla. This accelerates optimization without exposing the model to additional data and without altering the learning-rate schedule, and it is exactly the mini-batch reuse setting in which the SGD-form implicit regularization of Proposition 1 accumulates linearly over the T T steps within a fixed batch (Section 3.3 ).

sections.text: The 1000-epoch vanilla result lies between the 100-epoch vanilla baseline and frozen- ϕ \phi , closing 80 % 80\% of the inner-channel gap (from 0.914 0.914 MAE down to a residual 0.178 0.178 MAE relative to frozen- ϕ \phi ). [33] : per-step IGR accumulates over the optimization trajectory, so two settings that traverse comparable trajectory lengths exhibit comparable accumulated regularization. sections.heading: Appendix M Spectral metrics dissociate from task improvement
sections.text: A natural alternative explanation for the divergence between bilevel and static rewiring is spectral: that bilevel optimizes a graph-spectral objective (larger spectral gap λ 2 \lambda_{2} or narrower effective spectral support W ϵ W_{\epsilon} ) that static methods do not match. We tested this directly on six benchmarks. The data shows a clean dissociation between graph-spectral metrics and task improvement: GTR maximizes λ 2 \lambda_{2} on every benchmark by an order of magnitude yet produces no MAE gain, while bilevel achieves the largest forecasting gains on flow without maximizing λ 2 \lambda_{2} (and often decreasing it).

sections.heading: LCC-aligned measurement protocol.
sections.text: The standard ST adjacencies are highly fragmented under the threshold τ = 0.1 \tau=0.1 used by the standard implementation (35 components on PeMS04, 93 on PeMS07, 33 on AirQuality). Static rewiring methods that add edges (FoSR, BORF) merge components and change the largest connected component (LCC); whole-graph λ 2 \lambda_{2} is identically zero for any disconnected graph and is therefore an uninformative quantity. We restrict every comparison to the original-graph LCC node subset: spectra are computed on the subgraph induced by the LCC of the unmodified adjacency, identical for every method. Bilevel preserves LCC structure exactly on all bilevel runs (incremental edge reweighting does not change connectivity); static methods that connect new components are evaluated on the restricted subset, dropping any newly-added inter-component edges. Whole-graph λ 2 \lambda_{2} is reported separately in Table 10 .

Bilevel decreases λ 2 \lambda_{2} on four of six datasets, and where it increases (AirQuality), the increase does not produce a forecasting gain. The cross-method comparison against MAE (rightmost column, from Table 8 ) shows no relationship between λ 2 \lambda_{2} change and task improvement: GTR maximizes λ 2 \lambda_{2} everywhere with zero MAE gain, while bilevel produces − 3.8 -3.8 to − 6.4 % -6.4\% on flow datasets without raising λ 2 \lambda_{2} . sections.heading: Implication.
sections.text: GTR is a strong spectral-gap maximizer that produces no forecasting gain; bilevel produces the largest forecasting gains on flow without maximizing λ 2 \lambda_{2} or narrowing W ϵ W_{\epsilon} . Spectral gap optimization and effective-support narrowing are therefore dissociated from task improvement on these benchmarks. This does not contradict the worst-case propagation bounds of Topping et al. [35] , Di Giovanni et al. [11] , Marisca et al. [27] , which bound a different quantity (worst-case sensitivity, not task loss); it constrains the space of mechanistic explanations for the bilevel gain by ruling out a natural one. Combined with the inner-channel attribution (Sections 5.2 – 5.3 ), this strengthens the conclusion that the bilevel gain on flow forecasting is dominated by inner-loop training dynamics rather than by graph modification at the spectral level.

sections.heading: Appendix P Graph Distillation
sections.text: Frozen- ϕ \phi and graph distillation are complementary diagnostics with different scopes. Frozen- ϕ \phi measures the contribution of graph modification while holding inner-loop training constant : θ \theta is trained on A init A_{\mathrm{init}} with the same T T -step inner loop. Distillation measures the contribution of graph modification plus graph-model co-adaptation : θ \theta is re-trained from scratch on A ϕ A_{\phi} , partially reproducing the joint adaptation of θ \theta and A ϕ A_{\phi} that occurred during bilevel training. Two diagnostically distinguishable patterns follow. When bilevel optimization succeeds, distillation tends to exceed the frozen- ϕ \phi graph share by the magnitude of co-adaptation: on PeMS04 with DiffConv, distillation recovers 44 % 44\% of the bilevel gain while frozen- ϕ \phi assigns 22 % 22\% to the graph channel, locating the 22 22 -point gap as the empirical co-adaptation magnitude on this dataset. When bilevel optimization is blocked by an architectural scope condition, distillation can exceed direct bilevel because distillation bypasses the blocked optimization path: on DCRNN/PeMS04, direct bilevel improves vanilla by only − 0.5 % -0.5\% (within noise) while distillation of a DiffConv-learned graph improves by − 1.8 % -1.8\% . The two cases are not anomalies but expected signatures of the framework. By “co-adaptation” we mean the joint solution ( θ ∗ , A ϕ ∗ ) (\theta^{*},A_{\phi^{*}}) reached by the bilevel inner loop, in which θ ∗ \theta^{*} is tuned to the evolving A ϕ A_{\phi} at each outer iteration; distillation re-trains θ \theta from random initialization on the final A ϕ A_{\phi} , recovering only the portion of the joint solution that survives this re-initialization. sections.text: ChebConv shows mixed graph shares across flow datasets ( − 8 % -8\% on PeMS04, + 18 % +18\% on PeMS07, − 22 % -22\% on PeMS08), reflecting that a DiffConv-tuned adjacency is filter-specific and does not transfer cleanly across spatial filters; the variability is a property of the cross-backbone transfer rather than of the bilevel-learned adjacency itself.

sections.heading: Cora illustrates the conceptual distinction.
sections.text: Frozen- ϕ \phi attributes 63 % 63\% of the LDS gain to the graph channel on Cora (Table 1 ), while distillation recovers approximately 0 % 0\% at the modal binarization threshold (Table 20 , τ = 0.5 \tau{=}0.5 ). The gap is the empirical magnitude of θ \theta - A ϕ A_{\phi} co-adaptation: the bilevel inner loop builds GCN parameters jointly tuned to the evolving A ϕ A_{\phi} , and re-training a fresh GCN on the binarized A ϕ A_{\phi} does not reproduce this joint solution. Continuous-weight ST distillation does not require binarization and shows smaller co-adaptation gaps (PeMS04: frozen- ϕ \phi graph 22 % 22\% vs. distillation 44 % 44\% ), reflecting the same mechanism with the binarization step removed.

sections.heading: NC scope.
sections.text: We do not report graph distillation in the node classification regime as a same-protocol Table 14 entry: LDS produces Bernoulli edge probabilities rather than continuous edge weights, so any distillation procedure requires a binarization threshold whose choice strongly affects the result. NC distillation results across thresholds are reported separately in Table 20 .

sections.heading: Distillation as a method-agnostic fallback.
sections.text: Distillation extends the diagnostic scope to GSL methods outside the frozen- ϕ \phi control. Methods that satisfy the third precondition (positive clean-graph gain) but violate the first or second (e.g., single-level methods like IDGL, EM-based methods like GEN if they produced positive clean-graph gain) admit graph distillation as a method-agnostic complement. In our experiments, GEN and Pro-GNN do not produce positive clean-graph gain on Cora (Table 21 ), so neither diagnostic applies to those methods on the clean Cora graph; this is a property of the methods themselves, not of the diagnostic framework.

sections.heading: NC backbone configurations follow GSLB.
sections.text: We use GSLB’s released per-method configurations [ 21 ] without modification: the vanilla GCN baseline is a 2-layer GCN encoder (hidden 32 32 , row-normalized adjacency) and the LDS backbone is a 2-layer MetaDenseGCN (hidden 128 128 on Cora / 64 64 on Citeseer, symmetric D − 1 / 2 ( A + I ) D − 1 / 2 D^{-1/2}(A{+}I)D^{-1/2} normalization), reflecting GSLB’s published per-method tuning. The frozen- ϕ \phi control matches the LDS configuration exactly (same backbone class, hidden dim, normalization), differing only in whether the outer-loop graph parameter is updated. Consequently, in the NC regime the vanilla → \rightarrow frozen- ϕ \phi comparison reflects the joint effect of (i) backbone capacity, (ii) normalization, and (iii) inner-loop dynamics under GSLB’s per-method convention; the frozen- ϕ → \phi\rightarrow bilevel comparison, which isolates the graph channel cleanly under matched architecture, is unaffected by this convention. ST experiments do not exhibit this asymmetry: vanilla, frozen- ϕ \phi , and bilevel share the same DiffConv backbone, so the ST inner share is a clean attribution.

sections.heading: Appendix X Three-precondition framework
sections.text: This appendix develops the three-precondition framework introduced in Section 5.4 , which predicts when bilevel graph structure learning produces forecasting benefit. Section X.1 states the preconditions formally. Section X.2 documents the AirQuality (AQ-437) adjacency anatomy that motivates precondition (iii). Section X.3 classifies the six spatio-temporal datasets by the framework. Section X.4 reports the modification-magnitude figure migrated from the main text, and Section X.5 consolidates the flow-versus-speed signal-type analysis.

sections.heading: X.1 Formal statement of the three preconditions
sections.text: Let G = ( V , E , A init ) G=(V,E,A_{\text{init}}) denote the predefined adjacency available to a spatio-temporal forecasting model on N N sensors, and let the underlying data generator induce a true relational structure between sensors. Let Φ \Phi denote the policy class for the bilevel adjacency parameterization (here, a static undirected reweighting of A init A_{\text{init}} ). Definition 1 (Three preconditions for bilevel-GSL benefit) . We say bilevel GSL is plausibly beneficial on G G for the prediction task if all three of the following hold. (i) Structural slack. The predefined adjacency A init A_{\text{init}} is suboptimal for the task-relevant relational structure. Operationally, structural slack is small when distance-based or domain-prescribed edges already align with the directions of large prediction error gradients, and large when task-coupled sensor pairs experience high commute time or low Dirichlet alignment under A init A_{\text{init}} [ 35 , 11 , 5 ] . (ii) Loss identifiability. The prediction loss has informative gradients with respect to graph parameters: ‖ ∇ ϕ ℒ val ​ ( θ ∗ ​ ( ϕ ) , A ϕ ) ‖ > τ \|\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}(\theta^{*}(\phi),A_{\phi})\|>\tau for some task-meaningful threshold τ \tau , when evaluated near A init A_{\text{init}} . Identifiability fails when per-node local effects (sensor-specific embeddings, time-of-day patterns, day-of-week patterns) absorb the spatially-extractable variance, leaving the loss flat in the structural direction [ 9 , 26 ] . (iii) Parametrization expressiveness. The static undirected adjacency class { A ϕ : ϕ ∈ Φ } \{A_{\phi}:\phi\in\Phi\} can in principle represent the true dependency. Expressiveness fails when the true dependency is directional, time-varying, or supported on connectivity that is structurally absent from A init A_{\text{init}} in a way no reweighting can recover. The three preconditions are individually necessary for a non-trivial forecasting gain from a bilevel update of the static undirected adjacency. They are stated as conditions on the adjacency and the loss, not on the bilevel optimization procedure itself: a procedure may fail to find the gain even when (i)–(iii) hold, but the gain cannot exist when any one fails. Empirically, joint satisfaction of (i)–(iii) predicts a positive gain on all flow benchmarks (Table 26 ).

sections.heading: Mapping to the six benchmark regimes.
sections.text: Flow-signal datasets (PeMS04/07/08) satisfy all three preconditions: distance-based highway adjacency is incomplete with respect to flow conservation, the squared-error loss on traffic counts is informative with respect to inter-sensor structural changes, and a static undirected reweighted graph is an adequate representation. Speed-signal datasets (METR-LA, PeMS-BAY) fail preconditions (i)–(ii): the distance graph is well-aligned with the kinematic-wave physics that governs speed propagation [ 22 ] (so (i) fails), and per-node embeddings absorb the residual variance in modern STGNN backbones (so (ii) fails by the local-effects mechanism of Cini et al. [9] ). AirQuality (AQ-437) fails precondition (iii) for the structural reason analyzed in Section X.2 .

sections.heading: Distinguishing data limits from optimization limits.
sections.text: Failures of bilevel GSL on clean benchmarks admit two distinct diagnoses: (a) the predefined adjacency carries little exploitable slack and no procedure can recover gains beyond the inner channel (data limit), or (b) sufficient slack exists but the gradient-based outer loop fails to find it (optimization limit). The decomposition toolkit distinguishes them. When frozen- ϕ \phi , distillation, and end-to-end reweighting all converge on near-zero graph contribution (PeMS07: 101%, 1%, 5% respectively for the three diagnostics), the bottleneck is data; when they diverge (bilevel low but distillation high), the bottleneck is optimization. The corruption study on Cora provides the converse evidence: injected slack is captured approximately linearly by the bilevel procedure (graph channel grows from 0.56pp at r = 0.10 r{=}0.10 to 5.37pp at r = 0.75 r{=}0.75 ), demonstrating that the optimizer is not the binding constraint when slack exists. We therefore interpret the small graph channel on clean Cora and the near-zero graph channel on PeMS07 as data-limit regimes rather than optimizer failures.

sections.heading: Block-diagonal structure.
sections.text: The standard adjacency contains 2,699 edges, mean degree 12.4 12.4 , and 33 connected components : of these, 14 are isolated singletons and the remaining 19 form urban clusters that under single-linkage at 80 km collapse to 13 distinct cities. Every one of the 2,699 retained edges connects two stations within the same urban cluster ; the adjacency contains zero inter-city edges . The intra-city weight median is 0.47 0.47 and the inter-city weight is exactly zero, making the AQ-437 adjacency strictly block-diagonal under the canonical bandwidth choice. The mechanism is that intra-Beijing pairwise distances lie around 20 20 to 30 30 km (matching θ = 26.1 \theta=26.1 km), while inter-city distances exceed several hundred kilometers; the ratio d 2 / θ 2 d^{2}/\theta^{2} for inter-city pairs reaches values of several hundred, driving the Gaussian kernel below the τ = 0.1 \tau=0.1 threshold for every inter-city pair.

sections.heading: Reasons no static undirected reweighting can repair this.
sections.text: A bilevel reweighting policy A ϕ = A init ⊙ π ϕ A_{\phi}=A_{\text{init}}\odot\pi_{\phi} scales existing edges; it cannot create edges that the threshold operation ( 5 ) excluded. The 33 components are therefore frozen in the policy class, and any propagation between cities requires either edge addition (outside the Φ \Phi used in the bilevel ST setting) or non-static parameterization (outside the precondition (iii) class). This is the structural reason precondition (iii) fails on AQ-437 and bilevel produces no forecasting benefit, despite producing the largest median modification magnitude across the six benchmarks (Section X.4 ).

sections.heading: Connection to the framework.
sections.text: The anti-correlation aligns with the precondition diagnosis: on flow datasets where preconditions (i)–(iii) hold, bilevel applies selective minimal intervention to a graph already close to the task-relevant structure. On AirQuality where (iii) fails, bilevel applies aggressive modification ( | Δ ​ w | |\Delta w| outliers reach ∼ 25 \sim 25 ) that does not translate to forecasting benefit, consistent with policy-class limits rather than insufficient modification effort. This is the structural counterpart of precondition (iii): a parametrization that cannot represent the true dependency cannot produce the gain regardless of the modification budget the optimizer expends.

sections.heading: X.5 Flow versus speed signal pattern
sections.text: The flow/speed split observed across the four PeMS datasets aligns with preconditions (i)–(ii) in the framework. Flow-signal sensors record vehicle counts that obey approximate flow conservation across road segments: a perturbation at one sensor propagates as a wave whose direction and amplitude depend on inter-sensor connectivity beyond geometric distance. The static distance-based adjacency carries non-trivial structural slack with respect to this connectivity (precondition (i) holds), and the squared-error loss is informative with respect to inter-sensor structural changes because flow signals couple across sensors more strongly than per-node temporal patterns can absorb (precondition (ii) holds). Speed-signal sensors record per-segment vehicle velocity, which under the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards (LWR) kinematic-wave model [ 22 ] propagates locally along the road network with shockwaves whose speed and direction are determined by physical road geometry. The distance graph is therefore well-aligned with the dynamics (precondition (i) fails: structural slack is small), and per-node temporal patterns (rush-hour, weekday/weekend, holiday) account for the dominant fraction of the observed variance in modern STGNN backbones [ 9 ] (precondition (ii) fails: the loss is flat in the structural direction). The flow/speed boundary is therefore not signal type per se but the alignment of the distance graph with the underlying transport physics, mediated by the share of variance absorbed by sensor-local effects.

sections.heading: Empirical confirmation.
sections.text: On flow datasets (PeMS04/07/08), bilevel achieves between − 3.8 % -3.8\% and − 6.4 % -6.4\% MAE improvement with complete distributional separation across seeds. On speed datasets (METR-LA, PeMS-BAY), bilevel produces − 0.7 % -0.7\% and + 2.5 % +2.5\% respectively, and the frozen- ϕ \phi control on METR-LA is also worse than vanilla, indicating that the inner channel itself fails on speed signals rather than being canceled by a harmful outer update. This is the empirical signature predicted by the framework when preconditions (i)–(ii) fail: neither the inner channel (no structural information to extract) nor the outer channel (no informative gradient) produces benefit.

We find that this attribution may be overstated: training-dynamics effects in the inner loop, rather than the rewiring itself, capture a substantial share of the gain. To establish this, we introduce frozen- ϕ \phi , a control that freezes the graph while retaining the inner-loop training schedule. This decomposes the bilevel gain into an inner channel of T T -step training dynamics with implicit gradient regularization and a graph channel of the graph rewiring itself. On spatio-temporal flow forecasting the inner channel matches or exceeds the full bilevel pipeline, accounting for 78 78 – 101 % 101\% of the gain; on node classification it accounts for 37 37 – 44 % 44\% under a Bernoulli edge-level parameterization. We also verify that classical spectral diagnostics can dissociate from task gain. We propose frozen- ϕ \phi as a standardized diagnostic for bilevel graph structure learning, with graph distillation as a method-agnostic complement. A three-precondition framework further predicts the sign of the bilevel gain on all six benchmarks. 1 Introduction Bilevel graph structure learning (GSL) optimizes the graph and the model jointly through an outer loop on a validation objective, and the learned adjacency is credited with the resulting improvement [ 13 , 6 ] . The bilevel procedure differs from vanilla training in two ways that could each account for its reported gain. The first is graph modification, executed by the outer loop. The second is an inner loop that runs T T gradient steps per outer iteration, which has known implicit regularization properties [ 4 , 33 ] unrelated to the graph. Existing evaluations treat the bilevel gain as flowing entirely from the first mechanism. We ask whether this attribution is correct. We introduce the frozen- ϕ \phi control : the same bilevel training loop, with the same T T -step inner optimization and warmup schedule, but with the graph parameter ϕ \phi held fixed at its initial value. The control isolates extended inner optimization from graph modification, holding every other variable constant. This is the GSL analogue of the frozen-controller experiments that prompted reassessment of attribution in neural architecture search, where freezing the architecture parameter while preserving the training pipeline revealed that pipeline choices, rather than searched architectures, explained much of the gain [ 19 , 40 ] . Our goal is to reframe which component of bilevel GSL is actually responsible for the improvement. A productive theoretical framework has characterized over-squashing through graph curvature [ 35 ] , commute time and effective resistance [ 11 , 5 ] , and the spatio-temporal Jacobian factorization for decoupled STGNNs [ 27 ] . Our decomposition is complementary to this framework: the over-squashing bounds describe worst-case sensitivity propagation between nodes, while our control measures how much of bilevel’s empirical performance lift is attributable to graph modification at all. Contributions. Our contributions are as follows. 1. We show that, across both spatio-temporal flow forecasting and node classification, a substantial fraction of reported bilevel-GSL gains is attributable to inner-loop training dynamics rather than to the learned graph structure, with the inner channel accounting for 78 78 – 101 % 101\% on flow forecasting and 37 37 – 44 % 44\% on node classification. 2. We corroborate this attribution through three independent diagnostics (edge corruption that varies graph quality, alternative training schedules including weight decay and end-to-end joint training, and convergent triangulation on PeMS07), complemented by a T T -sweep that distinguishes two inner-loop training regimes (mini-batch reuse versus full-batch reset), all unified by an implicit-gradient-regularization mechanism. 3. We propose frozen- ϕ \phi as a standardized diagnostic for gradient-based bilevel GSL that modifies rather than replaces the initial adjacency, with graph distillation as a method-agnostic complement, accompanied by a three-precondition framework on the predefined adjacency that predicts when bilevel rewiring helps. What this paper does not claim. We do not claim that learned graph structure is useless in bilevel GSL, nor that bilevel methods cannot be improved; we claim that, under standard reporting practice, the inner loop’s contribution to measured gains is much larger than typically credited. 2 Related Work Bilevel and related graph structure learning. Bilevel GSL parameterizes the adjacency jointly with model weights via nested optimization with an outer validation objective. LDS [ 13 ] introduced a per-edge Bernoulli parameterization; IDGL [ 6 ] iteratively learns a continuous adjacency from multi-head weighted cosine similarity of node embeddings under a single (non-nested) training objective. GEN [ 38 ] uses EM-based alternation, and Pro-GNN [ 17 ] couples graph learning with adversarial defense (gains primarily on perturbed graphs). LCGS [ 15 ] is the closest prior bilevel method using a continuous (dual-normalized) adjacency rather than LDS’s Bernoulli parameterization, with head-to-head comparison against LDS on Cora and Citeseer. Single-level alternatives [ 12 , 25 , 32 ] and ST-domain analogues [ 16 , 42 , 34 , 10 , 26 ] use joint training rather than bilevel optimization. Adaptive STGNNs internalize graph learning into the forward pass: AGCRN [ 2 ] uses an embedding-based internal adjacency, while GraphWaveNet [ 39 ] uses such an internal matrix alongside diffusion (random-walk normalized) transitions of a pre-defined adjacency. The frozen- ϕ \phi decomposition is defined specifically for bilevel GSL with gradient-based outer updates and incremental graph modification (Section 3 ); single-level and adaptive approaches lie outside this scope. Over-squashing and graph rewiring. Alon and Yahav [1] identified over-squashing in message-passing networks. Subsequent theory connected the phenomenon to graph curvature [ 35 ] , information contraction [ 3 ] , commute time [ 11 ] , and effective resistance [ 5 ] , motivating task-agnostic rewiring preprocessors [ 14 , 18 , 28 , 5 ] . Tori et al. [36] found that curvature-based rewiring gains often reflect hyperparameter sweep outliers, underscoring the importance of controlled evaluation. Marisca et al. [27] extended the framework to spatio-temporal GNNs with a layer-wise multiplicative Jacobian factorization for time-then-space and time-and-space architectures, the structural foundation on which our architectural scope conditions rest. Our methodology shares the controlled-evaluation principle of Tori et al. [36] but isolates a distinct confound: the inner-loop training schedule, rather than hyperparameter sensitivity, in the bilevel optimization regime. The attribution gap. No prior study has isolated the contribution of graph modification from the training dynamics introduced by bilevel optimization, despite extensive theoretical and empirical work on graph rewiring. Recent benchmarks [ 21 , 44 ] independently observe that GSL methods do not consistently outperform vanilla GNN counterparts on standard benchmarks, but do not identify the mechanism. The six-dataset gain pattern admits a unified explanation through three preconditions on the predefined adjacency: (i) structural slack ( A init A_{	ext{init}} is suboptimal for the task-relevant structure), (ii) loss identifiability (the validation loss has informative gradients in ϕ \phi near A init A_{	ext{init}} ), and (iii) parametrization expressiveness (the policy class can represent the true dependency); formalized in Appendix X.1 , per-dataset mapping in Table 26 . Flow datasets satisfy all three; speed datasets fail (i)–(ii) because kinematic-wave physics [ 22 ] aligns the distance graph with the dynamics and per-node embeddings absorb the residual variance; AirQuality fails (iii) because the standard distance-based adjacency is block-diagonal with zero inter-city edges (Appendix X.2 ). The framework correctly predicts the sign of the bilevel gain on all six benchmarks, including the three on which bilevel does not improve over the clean-graph baseline; Appendix X.6 summarizes the resulting practitioner decision flow. Methodological recommendation. We propose the frozen- ϕ \phi ablation as a standard control in graph structure learning. Concretely, any paper reporting gains from a learned graph should report: (i) the frozen- ϕ \phi test metric under the same T T -step inner schedule as the full bilevel method, (ii) the inner share Δ inner / Δ total \Delta_{\mathrm{inner}}/\Delta_{\mathrm{total}} from ( 2 ), (iii) a T T -sweep checking whether the frozen- ϕ \phi result is T T -dependent or T T -invariant. Absent these controls, reported GSL gains are confounded with training dynamics introduced by the inner optimization schedule. For methods outside the scope of the frozen- ϕ \phi control, graph distillation provides a method-agnostic complement (Appendix P ). Relation to bilevel optimization beyond GSL. Implicit regularization in bilevel optimization has been studied in meta-learning [ 37 , 31 ] . Our contribution is not to discover this phenomenon but to (i) show that it explains a substantial share of gains attributed to graph modification in bilevel GSL, where this attribution has not been previously questioned, and (ii) provide a diagnostic that GSL practitioners can run on their own methods. The diagnostic principle, isolating outer-parameter contribution by freezing the outer parameter while preserving inner-loop training, potentially applies to bilevel optimization beyond GSL, though we leave such extensions to future work.
